approaches.title: Pterional (frontotemporal) craniotomy
approaches.summary: The workhorse anterolateral approach: a frontotemporal flap centred on the pterion, drilling of the sphenoid ridge and opening of the sylvian fissure give access to the anterior circle of Willis, optic apparatus and parasellar region.
indications: Anterior circulation aneurysms (ICA, posterior communicating, anterior choroidal, MCA, many anterior communicating)
Sellar/parasellar and suprasellar tumours with lateral extension
Sphenoid wing and clinoidal meningiomas
Anterior insular and frontotemporal lesions
approaches.position: Supine in pins. Head elevated above the heart, rotated to the opposite side, typically about 30–45° depending on the target and the surgeon (more for anterior and midline targets, less for posterior targets such as the basilar apex), and extended so the malar eminence is the highest point and the frontal lobe falls away from the orbital roof.

steps.t: Curvilinear incision starting at the zygomatic arch about 1 cm in front of the tragus, running up behind the hairline to the midline or mid-pupillary line. Stay close to the tragus to spare the frontal branch of the superficial temporal artery and the facial nerve branches.

Reflect the scalp flap. Protect the frontal branch of the facial nerve with interfascial or subfascial dissection of the temporalis fascia. Elevate temporalis muscle and retract it inferiorly and posteriorly.

Burr holes (classically at the keyhole behind the frontozygomatic suture and on the squamous temporal bone) and a frontotemporal flap centred on the pterion. Drill the lateral sphenoid ridge flat down towards the superior orbital fissure so the view along the skull base is unobstructed.
Open the dura in a curve based on the sphenoid ridge. Release CSF from the basal cisterns (carotid, optic, lamina terminalis) to relax the brain before any retraction.

Split the sylvian fissure from distal to proximal or proximal to distal, keeping the superficial sylvian veins with the temporal side where possible, and follow the MCA branches down to M1 and the ICA bifurcation.
Deep working spaces: optico-carotid, carotid-oculomotor and the space above the ICA bifurcation. Proximal ICA control is obtained before aneurysm dissection.
Watertight dural closure, bone flap fixation, anatomical re-suspension of temporalis to limit temporal hollowing.

risks.label: Right MCA M1–M2 and lenticulostriate perforators
risks.why: Perforator injury gives capsular infarction; branch occlusion infarcts eloquent cortex.

risks.label: Right ICA (supraclinoid)
risks.why: Proximal control point; posterior communicating and anterior choroidal arteries arise here.

risks.label: Optic chiasm and right optic nerve
risks.why: Mobilised structures in the optico-carotid window; direct or vascular injury causes visual loss.

risks.label: Right temporalis
risks.why: Denervation or devascularisation causes atrophy and cosmetic hollowing.

risks.label: Frontal branch of facial nerve
risks.why: Runs in the superficial fat pad over the temporalis fascia above the zygomatic arch (not modelled).

pearls: Brain relaxation comes from CSF release, not retraction.
Flattening the sphenoid ridge shortens the working distance more than enlarging the flap.
pitfalls: Too much head rotation lets the temporal lobe fall into the field.
Tearing bridging sylvian veins can cause venous congestion.

approaches.title: Orbitozygomatic approach
approaches.summary: A pterional exposure extended by removing the superolateral orbital rim, part of the orbital roof and the zygomatic arch. The lower bone margin gives a more basal, upward-looking view with less brain retraction.
indications: High-riding basilar apex and upper basilar aneurysms
Large sellar, parasellar and cavernous sinus tumours
Upper clival and interpeduncular lesions
Orbital and orbitocranial lesions
approaches.position: As for pterional, with rotation and extension adjusted to the target.

steps.t: Extended frontotemporal incision reaching further across the midline to allow wider reflection of the scalp flap.
Subfascial dissection to expose the orbital rim and zygomatic arch; free the supraorbital nerve from its notch or foramen; strip the periorbita from the orbital roof and lateral wall.
Raise a standard pterional flap.
Osteotomies release the superolateral orbital rim, orbital roof and zygomatic arch as one piece or two pieces, protecting the periorbita and orbital contents.
Open the dura and use trans-sylvian and subfrontal corridors. The lowered bone margin lets the surgeon look up to the basilar apex through the carotid-oculomotor window.
Replace and plate the orbitozygomatic bar anatomically to prevent enophthalmos and facial asymmetry.

risks.label: Basilar apex and posterior cerebral perforators
risks.why: The thalamoperforating arteries arising at the apex are the main source of serious morbidity.

risks.label: Right ICA and optic nerve
risks.match: right internal carotid artery, intracranial|right optic nerve
risks.why: They border the working windows.

risks.label: Orbital contents
risks.match: right eyeball|right lateral rectus|right superior rectus
risks.why: Periorbital breach leads to fat herniation and later enophthalmos.

risks.label: Right oculomotor nerve
risks.why: Crosses the carotid-oculomotor window; shown from population tractography, so its course is approximate.

pearls: Choose the orbitozygomatic extension when the target sits high above the dorsum sellae or the working angle through a pterional flap is too steep.
pitfalls: Poor bar reconstruction produces visible cosmetic deformity and enophthalmos.

approaches.title: Supraorbital keyhole (eyebrow) approach
approaches.summary: A small frontobasal craniotomy through an eyebrow incision, flush with the orbital roof, giving a subfrontal corridor to the anterior circle of Willis and chiasmatic region with limited soft-tissue disruption.
indications: Selected anterior communicating and ICA aneurysms
Small olfactory groove, planum and tuberculum lesions
Selected suprasellar lesions
approaches.position: Supine, head extended so the frontal lobe falls away from the orbital roof, and rotated towards the opposite side by an amount that depends on the target.

steps.t: Incision within the eyebrow, lateral to the supraorbital notch to protect the supraorbital nerve.
Small frontobasal craniotomy placed as low as possible on the orbital rim; drill down the inner table and orbital roof ridges to widen the view without enlarging the skin opening.
Open the dura, release CSF from the chiasmatic and carotid cisterns and work along the orbital roof. Angled endoscopes can inspect areas hidden from the microscope.

risks.label: Anterior communicating complex
risks.why: Target area; perforators and the recurrent artery of Heubner arise here.

risks.label: Optic chiasm
risks.why: Lies immediately below the working space.

risks.label: Supraorbital nerve and frontalis branch
risks.why: Forehead numbness or eyebrow weakness if injured (not modelled).

risks.label: Frontal sinus
risks.why: Opening it risks CSF leak and infection; check preoperative CT (not modelled).

pearls: Case selection matters: the keyhole trades working freedom for smaller access, so rehearse the trajectory on imaging.
pitfalls: A flap placed too high loses the basal view; a large frontal sinus may make the approach unsuitable.
approaches.schematic: Flap position is drawn on this skull; the size of a keyhole opening varies between surgeons.

approaches.title: Bifrontal subfrontal approach
approaches.summary: A bicoronal incision and low bifrontal craniotomy give broad access to the anterior cranial fossa floor from both sides of the falx.
indications: Olfactory groove and large planum meningiomas
Anterior skull-base tumours and repairs
Selected suprasellar and third-ventricle lesions via lamina terminalis
approaches.position: Supine, head neutral and slightly extended.

steps.t: Incision behind the hairline from one zygomatic root to the other. Preserve a vascularised pericranial flap for skull-base reconstruction.
Low bifrontal craniotomy close to the anterior fossa floor. If the frontal sinus is opened, cranialise it: remove the mucosa and occlude the ducts.
Open the dura above the orbital roofs. The anterior superior sagittal sinus and falx may be ligated and divided at the front to join the two sides.
Work along the anterior fossa floor, devascularising tumour from its base early. Identify the anterior cerebral arteries and optic apparatus behind large tumours.
Repair skull-base defects and cover the cranialised sinus with the pericranial flap.

risks.label: Superior sagittal sinus and bridging veins
risks.why: Division is limited to the anterior segment; posterior venous injury can cause venous infarction.

risks.label: Anterior cerebral arteries
risks.why: Often displaced or encased by large anterior fossa tumours.

risks.label: Olfactory tracts
risks.why: Loss of smell if both are damaged (not modelled).

risks.label: Frontal lobes
risks.why: Retraction injury and oedema affect behaviour and executive function.

pearls: Early devascularisation at the skull base reduces bleeding from anterior fossa meningiomas.
pitfalls: Unrecognised frontal sinus entry leads to CSF leak and infection.

approaches.title: Anterior interhemispheric transcallosal approach
approaches.summary: A parasagittal frontal craniotomy, dissection down the interhemispheric fissure and a short callosotomy lead into the lateral ventricle and, through the foramen of Monro, the third ventricle without crossing cortex.
indications: Colloid cysts and other third-ventricle lesions
Intraventricular tumours of the lateral ventricle body and frontal horn
Selected thalamic lesions reaching the ventricle
approaches.position: Supine with the head neutral and flexed, or with the head turned so the dependent hemisphere falls away by gravity.

steps.t: Linear or U-shaped scalp incision over the coronal suture, crossing the midline.
Parasagittal flap mostly anterior to the coronal suture, reaching the superior sagittal sinus. This keeps the approach in front of motor cortex and between the bridging veins.
Open the dura towards the sinus, preserve bridging veins, and dissect down the fissure to the corpus callosum, identifying the paired pericallosal arteries.
Make a short midline opening in the callosal body to enter the lateral ventricle.

Identify the foramen from the choroid plexus, the thalamostriate and septal veins, and the column of the fornix. Enlarge access to the third ventricle by transforaminal, transchoroidal or interforniceal routes as needed.

risks.label: Bridging veins and superior sagittal sinus
risks.why: Sacrificing several bridging veins risks venous infarction.

risks.label: Pericallosal arteries
risks.why: Lie on the corpus callosum and must be separated, not damaged.

risks.label: Fornix
risks.why: Bilateral forniceal injury causes severe memory loss.

risks.label: Thalamostriate vein and caudate/thalamus
risks.match: right caudate nucleus|right anterior thalamic nucleus
risks.why: Venous injury at the foramen can infarct the basal ganglia.

risks.label: Supplementary motor area and frontal aslant tract
risks.match: right superior frontal gyrus|frontal aslant tract r
risks.why: Retraction can produce a transient SMA syndrome; the frontal aslant tract runs from the SMA region to the inferior frontal gyrus.

pearls: Plan the flap on venous imaging to fit between bridging veins.
Confirm the side of the ventricle entered by following the thalamostriate vein and choroid plexus to the foramen.
pitfalls: A long callosotomy risks disconnection syndromes.
approaches.schematic: Corridor and entry point are illustrative. The foramen of Monro target is placed from the registered atlas brain.

approaches.title: Subtemporal approach
approaches.summary: A low temporal craniotomy flush with the middle fossa floor; gentle elevation of the temporal lobe exposes the tentorial edge, ambient cistern and upper petroclival region.
indications: Low-lying basilar apex and P1–P2 or SCA aneurysms
Tentorial incisura and ambient cistern lesions
Upper petroclival lesions, combined with petrous drilling (see Kawase)
approaches.position: Lateral or supine with the head turned 90° and the vertex tilted slightly down so the temporal lobe falls away from the floor.

steps.t: Linear, question-mark or horseshoe incision centred over the zygomatic root.
Temporal craniotomy with the lower edge drilled flush with the middle fossa floor; wax any opened mastoid air cells.
Lumbar drain and osmotic therapy help. Elevate the temporal lobe gently while protecting the vein of Labbé.
Open the arachnoid of the ambient cistern. The tentorium can be divided behind the entry of the trochlear nerve to widen the view down to the upper clivus.

risks.label: Vein of Labbé
risks.why: Injury can cause temporal venous infarction, with aphasia on the dominant side (not modelled).

risks.label: Right PCA, SCA and basilar apex
risks.why: Main targets and at risk during dissection.

risks.label: Temporal lobe
risks.match: right inferior temporal gyrus|right fusiform gyrus|right parahippocampal gyrus
risks.why: Retraction contusion.

risks.label: Oculomotor nerve
risks.why: Runs towards the tentorial edge and cavernous sinus; the trochlear nerve along the tentorial edge is not modelled.

pearls: Choose the non-dominant side when possible.
Drain CSF before retracting.
pitfalls: Leaving a lip of bone at the floor forces extra temporal lobe retraction.
approaches.schematic: Target is set in the ambient cistern lateral to the midbrain on the registered brain.

approaches.title: Retrosigmoid (lateral suboccipital) approach
approaches.summary: A craniotomy behind the sigmoid sinus and below the transverse sinus opens the cerebellopontine angle; the cerebellum falls away medially after CSF release.
indications: Vestibular schwannoma and other CPA tumours
Microvascular decompression for trigeminal neuralgia and hemifacial spasm
Lateral brainstem and petrous-face meningiomas
approaches.position: Lateral (park-bench) or supine with the head turned; shoulder taped down so the mastoid region is uppermost.

steps.t: Linear or gently curved incision two fingerbreadths behind the mastoid.
The asterion approximates the transverse–sigmoid junction, but this varies, so neuronavigation or burr-hole confirmation is used.
Craniotomy or craniectomy exposing the inferior edge of the transverse sinus and the posterior edge of the sigmoid sinus. Wax mastoid air cells.
Open the dura parallel to the sinuses and release CSF from the cisterna magna or lateral cerebellomedullary cistern before retraction.
Cranial nerves lie in three levels: V above, VII/VIII in the middle, IX–XI below. AICA loops and the superior petrosal (Dandy) vein are key vascular relationships.
Watertight dura; seal air cells again to prevent CSF rhinorrhoea.

risks.label: Transverse and sigmoid sinuses
risks.why: Tears cause bleeding and air embolism; thrombosis can follow.

risks.label: Pons and middle cerebellar peduncle
risks.why: Medial limit of the angle.

risks.label: Facial and vestibulocochlear nerves
risks.match: facial nerve \(cn vii\) r|vestibulocochlear nerve \(cn viii\) r
risks.why: Main functional risks in CPA surgery; shown from population tractography, so positions are approximate.

risks.label: Trigeminal nerve
risks.why: Upper level of the angle; the target in microvascular decompression.

risks.label: AICA and petrosal vein
risks.why: Key vascular relationships in the angle (not modelled).

pearls: Release CSF early; a slack cerebellum removes most need for retraction.
pitfalls: Unsealed mastoid air cells are a common source of postoperative CSF leak.

approaches.title: Midline suboccipital, telovelar approach
approaches.summary: A midline suboccipital craniotomy with opening of the tela choroidea and inferior medullary velum reaches the fourth ventricle without splitting the vermis.
indications: Fourth-ventricle tumours (for example medulloblastoma and ependymoma)
Vermian and paramedian cerebellar lesions
Lesions of the dorsal medulla and obex region
approaches.position: Prone (Concorde) with the neck flexed, or sitting. Sitting improves venous drainage but increases the risk of air embolism.

steps.t: Midline incision from above the inion to about C2, dividing through the avascular midline raphe.
Suboccipital craniotomy from below the transverse sinus to the foramen magnum; remove the C1 posterior arch if the tonsils or lesion descend.
Y-shaped dural opening, controlling the occipital or marginal sinus.
Separate the tonsils, open the tela choroidea and inferior medullary velum, and elevate the tonsils and hemispheres to expose the fourth ventricle floor and lateral recesses.
Protect the floor with a cottonoid early. Facial colliculus and the hypoglossal and vagal trigones are eloquent.

risks.label: Floor of the fourth ventricle
risks.why: Cranial nerve nuclei; injury causes facial or gaze palsy and bulbar dysfunction.

risks.label: Dentate nuclei and superior cerebellar peduncle
risks.why: Injury to the dentate–superior peduncle outflow, especially bilaterally, is associated with cerebellar mutism.

risks.label: PICA branches
risks.why: Loop over the tonsils and supply the medulla (not modelled).

pearls: The telovelar route avoids vermian splitting, which has been linked to cerebellar mutism, though comparative studies have not consistently shown a lower mutism rate; dentate and superior peduncle involvement also matter.
pitfalls: Sitting position without air embolism monitoring.

approaches.title: Far-lateral (transcondylar) approach
approaches.summary: A lateral suboccipital craniotomy carried to the foramen magnum, plus a C1 hemilaminectomy and, if needed, partial condyle drilling, opens the ventrolateral foramen magnum and lower clivus.
indications: Ventral and ventrolateral foramen magnum meningiomas
Vertebral artery and PICA origin aneurysms
Lower clival and ventral medullary lesions
approaches.position: Park-bench with the head flexed, rotated towards the floor and tilted, opening the angle between mastoid and shoulder.

steps.t: Hockey-stick or inverted-U incision from the mastoid tip along the superior nuchal line and down the midline.
Reflect the muscles in layers to reach the suboccipital triangle.
Find the V3 segment in its groove on the C1 posterior arch, surrounded by a venous plexus. Control it before bone removal.
Lateral suboccipital craniotomy down to the foramen magnum, C1 hemilaminectomy, and drilling of the posterior condyle as far as the lesion requires. The hypoglossal canal lies above the condyle.
Open the dura close to the vertebral artery dural entry. The lateral trajectory reaches ventral to the medulla with minimal retraction.

risks.label: Right vertebral artery
risks.why: Lies on the C1 arch and enters dura at the foramen magnum.

risks.label: Medulla
risks.why: Must not be retracted.

risks.label: Lower cranial nerves and hypoglossal nerve
risks.why: Injury causes dysphagia, dysphonia and tongue weakness (not modelled).

risks.label: Craniocervical stability
risks.why: Excessive condyle resection can destabilise the joint.

pearls: Only as much condyle as needed: many lesions need little or none once the dura is opened laterally.
pitfalls: Bleeding from the condylar emissary vein and suboccipital venous plexus obscures the vertebral artery.

approaches.title: Supracerebellar infratentorial approach
approaches.summary: A midline suboccipital craniotomy below the torcula uses the natural gap between the tentorium and the upper cerebellum to reach the pineal region, keeping the deep veins above the working field.
indications: Pineal region tumours needing open resection or biopsy
Posterior third-ventricle and dorsal midbrain lesions
approaches.position: Sitting (gravity opens the corridor) or prone/Concorde; neck flexed so the surgeon's line of sight runs along the underside of the tentorium towards the pineal region (the tentorium roughly parallel to the floor when sitting).

steps.t: Midline incision from above the inion down to the upper cervical spine.
Expose the inferior edge of the transverse sinus and torcula.
Open the dura, coagulate bridging veins from the upper cerebellar surface to the tentorium, and let the cerebellum fall away.
Open the thickened arachnoid. The internal cerebral veins, basal veins and vein of Galen lie above and around the lesion and must be preserved.

risks.label: Deep venous system
risks.why: Injury to the vein of Galen complex is poorly tolerated (not modelled).

risks.label: Tectum and midbrain
risks.why: Dorsal midbrain injury causes Parinaud syndrome.

risks.label: Torcula and transverse sinuses
risks.why: Form the upper margin of the craniotomy.

pearls: Treat hydrocephalus first; ETV with endoscopic biopsy is often combined.
pitfalls: Venous air embolism in the sitting position needs precordial Doppler or TOE monitoring and a plan.
approaches.schematic: Target is the pineal body of the registered atlas brain.

approaches.title: Endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal approach
approaches.summary: An endoscope through the nostril, a posterior septectomy and wide sphenoidotomy lead to the sellar floor, which is opened to reach the pituitary fossa.
indications: Pituitary adenomas
Rathke cleft cysts and other sellar lesions
Sellar biopsy and decompression
approaches.position: Supine, head slightly extended and turned towards the surgeon, fixed in pins or a horseshoe when navigation is used; nasal decongestion.

steps.t: Lateralise the turbinates, identify the sphenoid ostium, and harvest a nasoseptal flap when a larger skull-base repair is anticipated.
Posterior septectomy and wide sphenoidotomy. Remove sphenoid septations with care, as they often lead to the carotid prominences.
Sellar floor in the centre; carotid prominences laterally; optic prominences and lateral optico-carotid recesses superolaterally; clival recess below.
Open the sellar floor and dura. Work from inferior to lateral to superior so the diaphragma descends last.
Reconstruct according to the CSF leak: layered repair, with a vascularised nasoseptal flap for high-flow leaks.

risks.label: Internal carotid arteries
risks.why: Paraclival and cavernous ICA form the lateral limits; injury is life-threatening.

risks.label: Pituitary gland and stalk
risks.why: Endocrine deficit and diabetes insipidus.

risks.label: Optic chiasm
risks.why: Above the diaphragma; at risk with suprasellar extension.

risks.label: Cavernous sinus
risks.why: Venous bleeding and cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2, VI (not modelled).

pearls: Confirm the midline repeatedly with navigation and the vomer/rostrum.
pitfalls: A narrow sphenoidotomy limits instrument movement and angled visualisation.
approaches.schematic: The corridor starts in front of the nasal aperture; nasal soft tissues are not modelled.

approaches.title: Extended endonasal transplanum–transtuberculum approach
approaches.summary: The sellar opening is extended upwards through the tuberculum sellae and planum sphenoidale, between the optic canals, to reach the suprasellar space from below.
indications: Craniopharyngioma
Tuberculum sellae and planum meningiomas
Suprasellar extension of pituitary lesions
approaches.position: As for the transsphenoidal approach.

steps.t: Bilateral nasal corridors with a nasoseptal flap raised at the start.
Remove the tuberculum and posterior planum between the medial optico-carotid recesses; the optic canals mark the lateral limits.
Open the dura above and below the superior intercavernous sinus, then control and divide it.
Identify the optic chiasm, superior hypophyseal arteries, pituitary stalk and A1/AComm complex. Dissect tumour away from the stalk and hypothalamus when safe.
Multilayer repair with a vascularised flap, since leaks are high-flow.

risks.label: Optic chiasm and nerves
risks.why: Main functional risk; the superior hypophyseal arteries supply the chiasm from below.

risks.label: Anterior communicating complex
risks.why: Lies above and in front of the chiasm.

risks.label: Pituitary stalk and hypothalamus
risks.why: Endocrine and hypothalamic morbidity.

pearls: Preserving the superior hypophyseal arteries matters as much as preserving the chiasm itself.
pitfalls: A CSF leak rate higher than in standard transsphenoidal surgery unless repair is meticulous.
approaches.schematic: The opening is drawn as a single patch over the tuberculum and planum of this skull.

approaches.title: Endoscopic endonasal transclival approach
approaches.summary: Drilling the clivus behind the sphenoid sinus and nasopharynx opens a ventral corridor to the prepontine space and ventral brainstem.
indications: Clival chordoma and chondrosarcoma
Ventral brainstem and petroclival lesions in selected cases
Lower clival lesions extending to the foramen magnum
approaches.position: As for the transsphenoidal approach; the lower clivus needs a more caudal trajectory through the nasopharynx.

steps.t: Wide sphenoidotomy; for the middle and lower clivus the nasopharyngeal mucosa and prevertebral muscles are divided.
Drill the clivus between the paraclival ICAs. The vidian canal leads to the petrous ICA and is a useful landmark.
The basilar venous plexus bleeds from the dura; the abducens nerve enters Dorello canal medial to the paraclival ICA.
The basilar artery and its perforators lie directly behind the clival dura.

risks.label: Basilar artery and perforators
risks.why: Directly behind the dura.

risks.label: Paraclival ICAs
risks.why: Lateral limits of bone removal.

risks.label: Pons
risks.why: Ventral surface is the deep limit.

risks.label: Abducens nerve
risks.why: Diplopia from injury at Dorello canal (not modelled).

pearls: Plan lateral limits on CT angiography; the paraclival ICAs converge towards the midline in some patients.
pitfalls: Intradural transclival work carries a high CSF leak risk.
approaches.schematic: Clival opening drawn on this skull; the vessels are atlas-derived and not patient-specific.

approaches.title: Anterior petrosal (Kawase) approach
approaches.summary: A subtemporal extradural route with drilling of the petrous apex (Kawase rhomboid) opens the upper petroclival region and posterior fossa from the middle fossa, avoiding the cochlea and petrous ICA.
indications: Upper and middle petroclival meningiomas
Trigeminal schwannomas spanning the middle and posterior fossae
Selected basilar trunk aneurysms
approaches.position: Supine with the head turned 90° (or lateral), vertex slightly down.

steps.t: Low temporal craniotomy flush with the middle fossa floor.

Elevate the dura from the floor from posterior to anterior. Coagulate and divide the middle meningeal artery at the foramen spinosum; identify the greater superficial petrosal nerve (GSPN), V3 and the arcuate eminence.
Drill the rhomboid bounded by the GSPN, the trigeminal nerve, the petrous ridge and the arcuate eminence/IAC region, staying clear of the cochlea and the horizontal petrous ICA.
Open the middle and posterior fossa dura, divide the superior petrosal sinus and the tentorium, and reach the petroclival region.

risks.label: Petrous ICA
risks.why: Lies beneath the GSPN.

risks.label: Pons and trigeminal nerve
risks.why: Petroclival lesions compress the pons and displace the trigeminal root.

risks.label: Cochlea and GSPN
risks.why: Hearing loss; dry eye; facial nerve traction via the GSPN (not modelled).

risks.label: Vein of Labbé
risks.why: Temporal venous infarction (not modelled).

pearls: Cutting the GSPN rather than pulling on it protects the geniculate ganglion.
pitfalls: Drilling too far posterolaterally enters the cochlea.
approaches.schematic: The drilled area is placed at the petrous apex estimated from the registered brainstem; exact petrous landmarks are not segmented on this CT mesh.

approaches.title: Presigmoid (retrolabyrinthine) approach
approaches.summary: A mastoidectomy that skeletonises the sigmoid sinus and preserves the labyrinth opens the presigmoid dura; combined with a temporal craniotomy and tentorial division it reaches both sides of the tentorium at the petroclival region.
indications: Petroclival meningiomas with supra- and infratentorial extension
Ventrolateral brainstem lesions
approaches.position: Supine with the head turned, or lateral.

steps.t: C-shaped retroauricular incision reaching above the ear.
Cortical mastoidectomy; skeletonise the sigmoid sinus and identify the semicircular canals, which are preserved in the retrolabyrinthine variant.
Add a craniotomy above the transverse sinus when combining supra- and infratentorial exposure.
Open the dura between the sigmoid sinus and the posterior semicircular canal, divide the superior petrosal sinus and the tentorium, and reach the petroclival region.

risks.why: Skeletonised and retracted.

risks.label: Facial nerve (mastoid segment) and labyrinth
risks.why: Facial palsy and hearing loss (not modelled).

risks.label: Pons and petroclival region
risks.why: Deep target.

pitfalls: A contracted mastoid or anteriorly placed sigmoid sinus narrows the presigmoid window.

approaches.title: Translabyrinthine approach
approaches.summary: Removes the mastoid and the labyrinth to reach the internal acoustic meatus and cerebellopontine angle from the side, with little or no cerebellar retraction, at the cost of all hearing in that ear.
indications: Vestibular schwannoma when useful hearing is absent or not realistically preservable, particularly larger tumours
Other cerebellopontine angle lesions centred on the internal acoustic meatus
approaches.position: Supine with the head turned away (or lateral), facial nerve monitoring; abdomen prepared for a fat graft.

steps.t: Postauricular C-shaped incision a few centimetres behind the ear crease.
Complete mastoidectomy: skeletonise the sigmoid sinus, the middle fossa dura (tegmen) and the sinodural angle; open the antrum and identify the lateral semicircular canal.
Drill the lateral, posterior and superior semicircular canals and open the vestibule, keeping the mastoid segment of the facial nerve covered by a thin layer of bone.

Skeletonise the meatus around most of its circumference. At the fundus the transverse (horizontal) crest divides the meatus into upper and lower halves; in the upper half the vertical crest (Bill’s bar) separates the facial nerve in front from the superior vestibular nerve behind.
Open the presigmoid dura, debulk the tumour and dissect it off the facial nerve under monitoring. Seal the aditus and middle ear and fill the defect with abdominal fat to prevent CSF leak.

risks.label: Facial nerve
risks.why: Identified early at the fundus; stretched and thinned by large tumours.

risks.label: Cochlear and vestibular nerves
risks.why: Hearing is sacrificed with the labyrinth.

risks.label: Sigmoid sinus and jugular bulb
risks.why: Skeletonised; a high jugular bulb narrows the approach.

risks.label: Anterior inferior cerebellar artery
risks.why: May loop toward or into the porus or meatus in a proportion of patients; injury risks brainstem and cerebellar infarction (not modelled).

risks.label: Pons
risks.why: Medial limit of tumour dissection.

pearls: Locates the facial nerve at the fundus regardless of tumour size, before the cisternal part is dissected.
A contracted mastoid, high jugular bulb or anterior sigmoid sinus narrows the window; depressing the bulb or retracting the sinus may be needed.
pitfalls: Hearing is always lost, so it is a poor choice when serviceable hearing remains and tumour size allows a hearing-preservation route.
Unsealed air cells or middle ear are the usual route for CSF otorhinorrhoea.

approaches.title: Transcochlear approach
approaches.summary: Extends the translabyrinthine route forward: the facial nerve is rerouted posteriorly and the cochlea and petrous apex are drilled, giving a wide lateral view of the petroclival region and the front of the brainstem.
indications: Large petroclival meningiomas, chordomas or chondrosarcomas when hearing is already lost
Lesions ventral to the brainstem extending toward the midline clivus
approaches.position: Supine with the head turned away or lateral; facial nerve monitoring.

steps.t: Extended postauricular incision; the external auditory canal is divided and closed as a blind sac.
Mastoidectomy and labyrinthectomy as for the translabyrinthine approach, with removal of the middle ear contents.
Decompress the facial nerve from the stylomastoid foramen to the meatus, divide the greater superficial petrosal nerve at the geniculate ganglion and transpose the nerve posteriorly.
Drill the cochlea and petrous apex toward the clivus, keeping the petrous carotid as the anterior limit and working posterior and medial to its genu and horizontal segment.
Open the dura to expose the petroclival region, the basilar artery and the ventral pons.

risks.label: Facial nerve
risks.why: Rerouting often leaves lasting facial weakness of moderate degree.

risks.label: Internal carotid artery (petrous)
risks.why: Lies just in front of the cochlea, separated only by thin bone, and forms the anterior limit of petrous drilling (petrous segment not modelled here).

risks.label: Basilar artery
risks.why: At the depth of the exposure.

risks.label: Abducens nerve
risks.why: Ascends the clivus into Dorello’s canal within the exposure (not modelled).

risks.label: Pons
risks.why: Ventral brainstem target and limit.

risks.label: Jugular bulb, inferior petrosal sinus and lower cranial nerves
risks.why: Inferior limit of the exposure; injury to nerves IX–XI affects swallowing and voice (not modelled).

risks.label: Trigeminal nerve at the petrous apex
risks.why: Superior-anterior limit of the petrous apex exposure.

pearls: Provides one of the widest lateral exposures of the clivus without brain retraction.
A transotic variant leaves the facial nerve in its canal to reduce facial morbidity, at the cost of a narrower view.
pitfalls: Facial nerve morbidity is the main price of the approach.
Inadequate closure of the eustachian tube and ear canal leads to CSF leak.

approaches.title: External ventricular drain at Kocher point
approaches.summary: A frontal burr hole at Kocher point and a catheter aimed at the ipsilateral foramen of Monro drain the frontal horn.
indications: Acute hydrocephalus
Intracranial pressure monitoring
Intraventricular haemorrhage (drainage and, where used, lysis)
approaches.position: Supine, head neutral and elevated; the right (usually non-dominant) side is chosen unless there is a reason not to.

steps.t: Kocher point is commonly described as about 11 cm behind the nasion and about 3 cm from the midline, near the mid-pupillary line and about 1 cm in front of the coronal suture.
Twist-drill or burr hole; open the dura and coagulate the pia.

Pass the catheter perpendicular to the skull, aiming in the coronal plane towards the ipsilateral medial canthus and in the sagittal plane towards the external auditory meatus. CSF is usually reached within about 5–6 cm of the outer table in adults, often sooner when the ventricles are enlarged; avoid repeated passes.
Tunnel the catheter away from the incision and secure it to reduce infection and dislodgement.

risks.label: Right frontal horn and foramen of Monro
risks.why: Target.

risks.label: Caudate head and thalamus
risks.match: right caudate nucleus|right anterior thalamic nucleus
risks.why: Deep malposition.

risks.label: Superior sagittal sinus
risks.why: A too-medial entry risks the sinus and bridging veins.

risks.label: Motor cortex
risks.why: A too-posterior entry.

pearls: Check the ventricle size and midline shift on the scan: small or shifted ventricles need image guidance.
pitfalls: Multiple passes increase haemorrhage risk.

approaches.title: Ventricular access at Keen point
approaches.summary: A posterior parietal entry about 2.5–3 cm above and behind the top of the pinna reaches the atrium (trigone) of the lateral ventricle.
indications: Ventricular catheter when a frontal route is unsuitable
Access to the trigone
approaches.position: Lateral or supine with the head turned.

steps.t: Measure from the top of the pinna; the skin landmark is approximate and varies with head shape.
Pass the catheter perpendicular to the cortical surface towards the atrium.

risks.label: Right atrium and choroid plexus
risks.why: Target; the glomus of the choroid plexus lies in the atrium.

risks.label: Inferior parietal lobule (language on the dominant side)
risks.match: right supramarginal gyrus|right inferior parietal lobule
risks.why: Avoid the dominant side.

risks.label: Optic radiation
risks.why: Runs in the lateral wall of the atrium; shown from population tractography.

pearls: Neuronavigation is used when possible.
pitfalls: Dominant-hemisphere entry risks language cortex.

approaches.summary: A parieto-occipital entry, about 6 cm above the inion and 3–4 cm from the midline, used for posterior ventricular catheters.
indications: Posterior (parieto-occipital) ventricular shunt catheters
Emergency ventricular access in the prone position
approaches.position: Prone, lateral or supine with the head turned.

steps.t: About 6 cm above the inion and 3–4 cm from the midline.
The catheter is passed into the atrium and body of the lateral ventricle; many surgeons aim it along the long axis of the ventricle towards the frontal horn. Conventions vary.

risks.label: Right lateral ventricle
risks.why: Target.

risks.match: right visual cortex|right cuneus|optic radiation r
risks.why: Visual field deficits.

pearls: A longer intraventricular catheter placed towards the frontal horn keeps the tip away from the choroid plexus.
pitfalls: Too lateral an entry risks the optic radiation.

approaches.summary: An occipital entry about 3 cm above the inion and 2 cm from the midline, reaching the occipital horn.
indications: Occipital horn access
Emergency ventricular drainage in the prone position
approaches.position: Prone or lateral.

steps.t: About 3 cm above the inion and 2 cm from the midline.
Pass the catheter forwards into the occipital horn.

risks.label: Transverse sinus and torcula
risks.why: Lie just below and medial to the entry.

risks.label: Visual cortex
risks.match: right visual cortex|right cuneus|right lingual gyrus
risks.why: Calcarine cortex lies close to the trajectory.

pearls: Know where the torcula is on the scan before choosing this point.
pitfalls: The occipital horn is variable: often small or asymmetric, and occasionally rudimentary.

approaches.title: Endoscopic third ventriculostomy (ETV)
approaches.summary: An endoscope passed through the frontal horn and foramen of Monro opens the floor of the third ventricle into the prepontine cistern, bypassing an obstruction at or below the aqueduct.
indications: Obstructive hydrocephalus, for example aqueductal stenosis or tectal/posterior fossa mass
Combined with endoscopic biopsy of pineal-region tumours
approaches.position: Supine, head neutral or slightly flexed.

steps.t: Plan the line from the floor, just in front of the mammillary bodies, through the foramen of Monro on sagittal MRI. Its exit on the skull gives the burr hole, usually near the coronal suture about 2.5–3 cm from the midline.
Enter the frontal horn and identify the foramen of Monro from the choroid plexus, septal and thalamostriate veins.
Pass through the foramen without levering against the fornix.

Perforate the floor in the midline between the infundibular recess in front and the mammillary bodies behind, then dilate with a balloon. Check that the membrane of Liliequist is open and the basilar artery visible in the prepontine cistern.

risks.label: Basilar artery and perforators
risks.why: Lie immediately below the floor.

risks.label: Fornix
risks.why: Injured by torque at the foramen of Monro.

risks.label: Hypothalamus and mammillary bodies
risks.why: Endocrine and memory effects.

pearls: A straight trajectory through the foramen to the stoma site avoids forniceal injury.
pitfalls: A thick or opaque floor, or an abnormal basilar position, makes perforation hazardous.
approaches.schematic: Entry is computed on this model as the extension of the line from the stoma site through the foramen of Monro; on this composite it lands about 1 cm behind the estimated coronal suture.

approaches.title: Deep brain stimulation: subthalamic nucleus
approaches.summary: A stereotactic trajectory from a burr hole near the coronal suture to the subthalamic nucleus. Planning combines direct MRI targeting with indirect coordinates relative to the AC–PC line.
indications: Parkinson disease with motor fluctuations or tremor
approaches.position: Stereotactic frame or frameless system; often awake for microelectrode recording and test stimulation, or asleep with image verification.

steps.t: Identify the target on MRI and check it against indirect coordinates. Commonly quoted starting values: roughly 11–13 mm lateral, 2–4 mm posterior and 4–5 mm below the mid-commissural point. These are conventions to verify against current references and the individual scan.
Choose an entry near the coronal suture, a few centimetres from the midline, that avoids sulci, cortical and ventricular vessels and, where possible, the ventricle.
Microelectrode recording and macrostimulation (or intraoperative imaging) confirm position and side-effect thresholds.
Place the lead, secure it at the burr hole, and connect to an implanted pulse generator.

risks.label: Subthalamic nucleus
risks.why: Target (dorsolateral motor part).

risks.label: Internal capsule
risks.why: Current spread gives tonic muscle contraction or dysarthria.

risks.label: Substantia nigra and red nucleus
risks.why: Deep and medial neighbours; oculomotor fibres pass nearby.

pearls: Trajectory angles vary with each patient's anatomy; the angles in this model are illustrative.
pitfalls: Transventricular trajectories have been associated with lead deviation and, in some series, a higher complication rate.

Choose an entry near the coronal suture, a few centimetres from the midline, that avoids sulci, cortical and ventricular vessels and, where possible, the ventricle.
Microelectrode recording and macrostimulation (or intraoperative imaging) confirm position and side-effect thresholds.
Place the lead, secure it at the burr hole, and connect to an implanted pulse generator.

risks.why: Target (posteroventral).

risks.label: Optic tract
risks.why: Lies below the target: phosphenes on stimulation.

approaches.title: Deep brain stimulation: ventral intermediate thalamus
approaches.summary: A stereotactic trajectory from a burr hole near the coronal suture to the ventral intermediate nucleus (posterior ventral lateral thalamus). Planning combines direct MRI targeting with indirect coordinates relative to the AC–PC line.
indications: Essential tremor
Tremor-dominant disorders
approaches.position: Stereotactic frame or frameless system; often awake for microelectrode recording and test stimulation, or asleep with image verification.

steps.t: Identify the target on MRI and check it against indirect coordinates. Commonly quoted starting values: roughly 14–15 mm lateral to the midline (or about 11 mm lateral to the third-ventricle wall), about a quarter of the AC–PC length (often about 5–6 mm) in front of the posterior commissure, at the AC–PC plane. These are conventions to verify against current references and the individual scan.
Choose an entry near the coronal suture, a few centimetres from the midline, that avoids sulci, cortical and ventricular vessels and, where possible, the ventricle.
Microelectrode recording and macrostimulation (or intraoperative imaging) confirm position and side-effect thresholds.
Place the lead, secure it at the burr hole, and connect to an implanted pulse generator.

risks.why: Posterior neighbour: paraesthesia on stimulation.

risks.why: Lateral neighbour.

approaches.title: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion, C5–C6
approaches.summary: A transverse neck incision and the avascular plane between the carotid sheath laterally and the trachea/oesophagus medially lead to the front of the cervical spine for discectomy and interbody fusion.
indications: Cervical radiculopathy or myelopathy from disc herniation or osteophytes
Selected single- or multilevel anterior compression
approaches.position: Supine, neck slightly extended, shoulders gently taped down for radiography.

steps.t: Transverse incision in a skin crease at the level confirmed on fluoroscopy. Right- and left-sided approaches are both used; the left recurrent laryngeal nerve has a more predictable course, which some surgeons prefer.
Divide platysma. Develop the plane medial to sternocleidomastoid and the carotid sheath and lateral to the strap muscles, trachea and oesophagus, down to the prevertebral fascia.
Place a marker in the disc and confirm the level radiographically. Elevate the longus colli on each side and place retractors beneath them.
Remove the disc and posterior osteophytes; open or resect the posterior longitudinal ligament as needed; decompress the foramina towards the uncovertebral joints.
Insert an interbody cage or graft, with or without an anterior plate.

risks.label: Right carotid artery and internal jugular vein
risks.match: right common carotid|right internal jugular vein
risks.why: Retracted laterally inside the carotid sheath.

risks.label: Thyroid gland and larynx
risks.why: Retracted medially; the superior and inferior thyroid vessels cross the field at some levels.

risks.label: Vertebral artery
risks.why: Lies lateral to the uncovertebral joint in the transverse foramen.

risks.label: Recurrent laryngeal nerve and oesophagus
risks.why: Hoarseness, dysphagia, perforation (not modelled).

pearls: Stay medial to the uncovertebral joints to protect the vertebral artery.
pitfalls: Postoperative neck haematoma can compromise the airway.
approaches.schematic: Neck skin and oesophagus are not modelled; the skin incision is placed at an approximate depth in front of the larynx.

approaches.title: Posterior cervical laminectomy with lateral mass screws (C3–C6)
approaches.summary: A midline posterior exposure, en bloc removal of the laminae and lateral mass screw fixation decompress the cord over several levels while preventing post-laminectomy kyphosis.
indications: Multilevel cervical spondylotic myelopathy with preserved or lordotic alignment
Ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament
Posterior compressive lesions
approaches.position: Prone, head in pins, neck neutral to slightly flexed; reverse Trendelenburg reduces venous bleeding.

steps.t: Midline incision along the spinous processes of the levels to be treated.
Subperiosteal exposure to the lateral edge of the lateral masses; preserve the facet capsules of levels not being fused.
Mark entry points at the centre of each lateral mass (just medial to it in some techniques) and drill laterally and cephalad (in this model about 30° lateral and 15° cephalad; techniques differ).
Troughs at the lamina–lateral mass junction on both sides; lift the laminae off en bloc.
Place screws and contoured rods; decorticate and graft the facets.

risks.label: Vertebral arteries
risks.why: Lie anterior to the lateral masses; a medially directed screw puts them at risk.

risks.label: Exiting nerve roots
risks.why: C5 palsy is a recognised complication after posterior decompression (not modelled).

risks.label: Spinal cord and dura
risks.why: Dural tear or cord injury during lamina removal (not modelled).

pearls: Lateral angulation keeps the screw away from the vertebral artery; cephalad angulation helps avoid the exiting nerve root.
pitfalls: Laminectomy without fusion can lead to kyphosis in susceptible patients.

approaches.title: Lumbar laminectomy (L4)
approaches.summary: Removal of the spinous process and lamina, with undercutting of the medial facets, decompresses the central canal and lateral recesses.
indications: Lumbar canal stenosis with neurogenic claudication
Central compressive lesions
approaches.position: Prone on a frame with the abdomen free to reduce epidural venous bleeding.

steps.t: Midline incision over the target level confirmed with fluoroscopy.
Subperiosteal elevation of the paraspinal muscles, preserving the facet capsules.
Remove the spinous process and lamina; resect ligamentum flavum; undercut the medial facets to open the lateral recesses; follow each traversing root into its foramen.
Keep enough pars interarticularis and facet joint to avoid iatrogenic instability.

risks.why: Over-resection causes pars fracture or instability.

risks.why: Dural tear and root injury (not modelled).

pitfalls: Thinning the pars too much.

approaches.title: Lumbar pedicle screw fixation (L4–L5)
approaches.summary: Screws passed through the pedicles into the vertebral bodies, joined by rods, provide three-column fixation.
indications: Instability (for example spondylolisthesis)
Fusion after decompression
Trauma, tumour and deformity
approaches.position: Prone on a frame, abdomen free; fluoroscopy or navigation.

steps.t: Conventional lumbar entry is near the junction of the transverse process and the lateral edge of the superior articular process.

Converge medially; convergence usually increases caudally (often roughly 10–15° at L4 and more at L5). This model uses a single illustrative 12°; confirm on the patient's imaging. Stay parallel to the superior endplate on the lateral view.
Probe, palpate the tract walls and floor, tap if needed.
Place screws into the anterior body short of the anterior cortex, then connect with rods.

risks.why: Medial or inferior breach injures the dura or nerve roots.

risks.label: Great vessels
risks.why: An anterior cortical breach risks the aorta, vena cava or iliac vessels (not modelled).

pearls: Medial wall breaches are the most consequential; check with palpation and imaging.
pitfalls: Entry too lateral with too little convergence exits the pedicle laterally.

approaches.title: Costotransversectomy (T9, right)
approaches.summary: A posterolateral route that removes the medial rib, transverse process and pedicle to reach the lateral and ventral thoracic canal without retracting the spinal cord.
indications: Thoracic disc herniation (selected)
Ventral or lateral epidural tumour
Vertebral body biopsy or corpectomy combined with posterior stabilisation
approaches.position: Prone.

steps.t: Paramedian (or curved midline) incision over the rib and transverse process of the level.
Expose and remove the transverse process and medial part of the rib, working subperiosteally to keep the pleura intact.
Follow the intercostal nerve to the foramen; remove the pedicle to open the lateral canal.
Reach the posterolateral vertebral body and ventral canal lateral to the cord; add posterior fixation when stability is compromised.

risks.label: T9 vertebra and canal
risks.why: The cord must never be retracted.

risks.label: Pleura
risks.why: Pneumothorax (not modelled).

risks.label: Segmental arteries
risks.why: The artery of Adamkiewicz usually arises in the lower thoracic region, more often on the left; check angiography when relevant (not modelled).

pearls: Unilateral bone removal can destabilise the segment; plan fixation.
pitfalls: Pleural tears are common; check before closure.

approaches.title: C1–C2 posterior fixation (Goel–Harms technique)
approaches.summary: Polyaxial screws in the C1 lateral masses and the C2 pedicles (or pars), joined by rods, fix the atlantoaxial joint; each side is placed independently, so reduction can be done through the rods.
indications: Atlantoaxial instability: odontoid non-union or unstable odontoid fractures unsuitable for an anterior screw, os odontoideum, rheumatoid or post-traumatic instability
Fixation after C1–C2 decompression or tumour resection
approaches.position: Prone in pins, neck neutral to slightly flexed; check C1–C2 alignment on fluoroscopy before draping.

steps.t: Midline incision from the occiput to C3 and subperiosteal exposure of the C1 posterior arch, the C2 lamina and the C1–C2 joints. Along the upper border of the C1 arch keep dissection within about 1.5 cm of the midline (less in children), where the vertebral artery lies in its groove.

Mobilise the C2 nerve root and control the venous plexus below the C1 arch. Enter the middle of the posterior lateral mass, converge modestly medially (commonly about 10–15 degrees) and, on lateral fluoroscopy, run roughly parallel to the C1 posterior arch toward the anterior tubercle, avoiding a steep upward path into the occipitocondylar joint.

Enter the superomedial part of the C2 lateral mass and follow the pedicle, typically around 15–25 degrees medially and 20–30 degrees upward, individualised from CT. A pars screw is shorter and steeper when the pedicle is too small.
Connect the screws with rods, correct alignment if needed, then decorticate and graft between the C1 arch and the C2 lamina.

risks.label: Vertebral arteries
risks.why: Lie in the groove on the upper surface of the C1 arch and pass through the C2 transverse foramen beneath the pars; a high-riding artery can rule out a C2 pedicle screw, so review CT angiography first.

risks.label: Internal carotid arteries
risks.why: Lie in front of the C1 lateral masses; screw length is chosen from CT, as overpenetration of the anterior cortex endangers them.

risks.label: C2 nerve root and venous plexus
risks.why: Brisk venous bleeding; the root is sometimes divided for access, leaving occipital numbness (not modelled).

risks.label: Spinal cord
risks.why: A medial breach of either screw enters the canal (not modelled here).

pearls: Measure the C2 pedicle width and trace both vertebral arteries on preoperative CT before choosing pedicle, pars or translaminar screws.
Placing screws before reduction lets the rods help reduce a subluxed C1–C2 joint.
pitfalls: At C2 a lateral or inferior breach endangers the vertebral artery; at either level a medial breach endangers the cord.
Too-long C1 screws can reach the internal carotid artery or hypoglossal nerve in front of C1.

approaches.title: Anterior cervical corpectomy C5 with reconstruction
approaches.summary: Removes the C5 vertebral body with the discs above and below to decompress the spinal cord behind it, then reconstructs C4–C6 with a cage or strut graft and an anterior plate.
indications: Cord compression behind the vertebral body: ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament, spondylosis with retrovertebral compression
Vertebral body fracture, tumour or osteomyelitis
approaches.position: Supine with the neck neutral to slightly extended, avoiding hyperextension in a myelopathic patient; shoulders drawn down gently for lateral fluoroscopy.

steps.t: Transverse skin-crease incision over C5 (an oblique incision along sternocleidomastoid for longer constructs).
Divide platysma and develop the plane medial to sternocleidomastoid and the carotid sheath and lateral to the trachea and oesophagus down to the prevertebral fascia; elevate longus colli.
Remove the C4–5 and C5–6 discs out to the uncovertebral joints, which mark the lateral limits of safe bone removal.

Remove the central C5 body in a trough roughly 15–18 mm wide, planned from preoperative CT and centred between the uncovertebral joints (the distance between the vertebral arteries varies, and a tortuous artery may lie closer to the midline). Thin and remove the posterior cortex and, where it is compressive and separable, the posterior longitudinal ligament; in OPLL adherent to dura the ossified ligament may be thinned and allowed to float forward instead.
Place a cage or strut graft from C4 to C6 and fix it with an anterior plate; consider posterior supplementation for longer or osteoporotic constructs.

risks.label: Vertebral arteries
risks.why: Lateral limit of the trough; drifting off the midline risks injury.

risks.label: Carotid sheath
risks.match: right common carotid|right internal jugular vein
risks.why: Retracted laterally throughout.

risks.label: Trachea, oesophagus and thyroid
risks.why: Retracted medially; oesophageal injury is rare but serious.

risks.label: Recurrent laryngeal nerve
risks.why: Hoarseness from retraction or injury (not modelled).

risks.label: Spinal cord
risks.why: Directly behind the posterior cortex and ligament (not modelled here).

risks.label: C5 nerve root palsy
risks.why: Deltoid or biceps weakness after decompression, typically appearing hours to days later; more frequent after corpectomy than after discectomy.

risks.label: Dural tear and CSF leak
risks.why: Especially in OPLL with dural ossification.

risks.label: Haematoma and airway compromise
risks.why: Neck swelling with stridor after surgery needs urgent wound opening.

risks.label: Sympathetic chain
risks.why: Lies on longus colli; dissecting too far laterally causes Horner’s syndrome.

pearls: Re-check both uncovertebral joints repeatedly to keep the trough centred.
Swallowing difficulty is common early after multilevel anterior surgery.
pitfalls: Graft subsidence or dislodgement is more frequent than after discectomy alone, especially for multilevel corpectomy.

approaches.title: Thoracic pedicle screws T10–T11
approaches.summary: Bilateral pedicle screws at T10 and T11 joined by rods. Thoracic pedicles are narrower and more variable than lumbar ones, so the entry point and trajectory need extra care.
indications: Thoracolumbar fractures
Instability from spinal metastases
Deformity correction
approaches.position: Prone on a radiolucent frame, abdomen free.

steps.t: Midline incision and subperiosteal exposure out to the tips of the transverse processes.

At the junction of the transverse process with the lateral edge of the superior articular process; at T10–T11 this is around the upper third to the midpoint of the transverse process, varying by level and patient.

Converge slightly medially (often around 5–10 degrees at this level) and stay parallel to the superior endplate (straight-forward) or angle caudally (anatomical). Probe and palpate the four walls and the floor of the track before tapping.
Confirm position on fluoroscopy, navigation or intraoperative CT and connect with rods.

risks.label: Spinal canal (medial wall)
risks.why: A medial (or inferior) breach enters the canal or foramen; at T10–T11 this is spinal cord with little room around it (not modelled).

risks.label: Pleura and lung
risks.why: A lateral breach beyond the rib head can cause pneumothorax or pleural injury (not modelled).

risks.label: Aorta and segmental vessels
risks.why: The aorta lies anterolateral to the vertebral body, usually on the left; overlong screws or a breach of the anterolateral body cortex put it and the segmental vessels at risk (not modelled).

risks.label: Pedicles of T10 and T11
risks.why: Small or rotated pedicles reduce the safe margin.

pearls: Thoracic pedicles are narrowest in the mid-thoracic spine and widen toward the thoracolumbar junction.
Navigation or intraoperative CT improves accuracy in small or rotated pedicles.
pitfalls: An in–out–in path through the rib–pedicle junction is accepted in small pedicles but may give somewhat less pull-out strength than a fully intrapedicular screw, though studies differ.

approaches.title: TLIF L4–L5 (left-sided)
approaches.summary: Transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion: a unilateral facetectomy opens the foramen so the disc can be cleared and an interbody cage placed through the transforaminal window (analogous to Kambin’s triangle), combined with bilateral pedicle screws.
indications: Degenerative spondylolisthesis with stenosis
Foraminal stenosis needing indirect height restoration
Recurrent disc herniation with instability
approaches.position: Prone on a frame that keeps lumbar lordosis.

steps.t: Midline incision, exposure to the transverse processes and placement of L4 and L5 pedicle screws; distract on the approach side.
Remove the L4 inferior and L5 superior articular processes on the approach side, exposing the exiting L4 root above and the traversing L5 root and dura medially.
Work in the triangle bounded by the exiting root, the traversing root and dura, and the L5 superior endplate; clear the disc and prepare the endplates without breaching them.
Pack graft and place an oblique cage across the midline, then add rods and compress to restore lordosis.

risks.label: Exiting L4 root
risks.why: Upper border of the working window; injury causes painful dysaesthesia (not modelled).

risks.label: Traversing L5 root and dura
risks.why: Medial border of the window (not modelled).

risks.label: Dura
risks.why: Tears are common during facetectomy and when retracting the traversing root; repair or seal to avoid a CSF fistula (not modelled).

risks.label: Great vessels in front of the disc
risks.why: An instrument through the anterior annulus can injure the iliac vessels or the caval confluence, which lie in front of L4–L5 (not modelled).

risks.label: L4 and L5 vertebrae
risks.why: Endplate injury leads to cage subsidence.

pearls: Removing the whole facet lets the cage pass lateral to the dura with little retraction of the thecal sac, compared with a posterior interbody approach.
pitfalls: Aggressive endplate preparation causes subsidence; a cage that sits too posterior can back out.

approaches.title: Klingler fibre dissection, left hemisphere (BraDiPho specimen 19)
approaches.summary: Twelve stages of a real Klingler fibre dissection of a left hemisphere, photographed and reconstructed in 3D, from intact cortex down to the stem of the ventral system. Matching tractography bundles appear at each stage so you can compare dissected fibres with tractography.

steps.t: The left hemisphere after removal of the meninges and surface vessels, before any white matter is dissected. Orient yourself first: sylvian fissure, central sulcus, the three frontal gyri and the temporal gyri. Every later step is a separate photogrammetric model of this same specimen, aligned in one frame, so you can rotate and compare stages.

Grey matter is scooped out of the sulcal depths while the gyral crowns are kept. This exposes the short U-shaped fibres that link neighbouring gyri, the most superficial layer of white matter, and shows how deep each sulcus runs.

Cortex over the posterior temporal, inferior parietal and lateral occipital region is removed. BraDiPho’s sequence for this specimen places the superficial posterior transverse system here: the vertical occipital fasciculus and the posterior (indirect) segment of the arcuate fasciculus, running vertically between the temporo-occipital and parietal cortex.

Removal extends over the parietal and posterior frontal lobes to show the fronto-parietal superior longitudinal system (SLF). The coloured patches are the dissectors’ own annotations at this stage: precentral–postcentral, precentral–supramarginal, precentral–angular and middle frontal–supramarginal fibres. Compare them with the SLF tractography.

The long fibres that arch around the end of the sylvian fissure from frontal to temporal cortex are followed. The annotations trace precentral–middle temporal and middle frontal–middle temporal fibres (the arcuate course) alongside fronto-parietal SLF connections. In the dominant hemisphere, stimulating this pathway during awake surgery classically produces phonemic paraphasias and repetition errors.

The frontal, parietal and temporal opercula and the insular cortex are taken down. Under the insula the main body of the ventral (inferior longitudinal) system appears: the inferior fronto-occipital and uncinate fasciculi crossing through the extreme and external capsules at the temporal stem. Stimulating the IFOF in the dominant hemisphere is classically associated with semantic paraphasias.
The frontal ends of the inferior fronto-occipital and uncinate fasciculi are followed into the inferior frontal and orbitofrontal region.
Frontal cortex and superficial fibres are removed further to follow the deeper, dorsal frontal projections of the ventral system.
The frontal lobe is now dissected to its pole, completing the ventral deep frontal projections.

Posteriorly, the occipital and temporal projections of the ventral system are followed toward the occipital pole and basal temporal lobe, where they run in the sagittal stratum together with the inferior longitudinal fasciculus and the optic radiation. Meyer’s loop of the optic radiation lies in the roof of the temporal horn, which is why anterior temporal resections can cause a contralateral upper quadrantanopia.
Deeper removal exposes the lentiform nucleus and the fibres of the internal capsule fanning into the corona radiata, the deep limit of most insular and opercular resections.

In the final stage the stem of the ventral system is engraved where it passes through the temporal stem beneath the lentiform nucleus, the narrow bottleneck connecting frontal, temporal and occipital lobes.

approaches.title: Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg)
approaches.summary: Infarction of the left dorsolateral medulla. Most often due to vertebral artery disease, less often isolated PICA occlusion. The signature is a crossed sensory pattern: face on the side of the lesion, body on the other side.
context: ^(middle cerebellar peduncle|superior cerebellar peduncle|inferior cerebellar peduncle [lr])$

steps.t: Dorsolateral medulla, supplied by penetrating branches of the vertebral artery and the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA; not modelled). The red sphere marks the lesion site.

Spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract: loss of pain and temperature on the same (left) side of the face. Lateral spinothalamic tract: loss of pain and temperature on the opposite (right) side of the body. Neither pathway is modelled here; both run through the marked region.

Nucleus ambiguus: dysphagia, hoarseness, ipsilateral palatal and vocal-cord weakness. Vestibular nuclei: vertigo, nystagmus, nausea and vomiting. Inferior cerebellar peduncle (glowing) and any PICA-territory cerebellum: ipsilateral limb ataxia and lateropulsion.
Descending central sympathetic fibres pass through the lateral medulla: ipsilateral miosis, mild ptosis and sometimes facial anhidrosis. The fibres are not modelled.
The pyramid (corticospinal tract) and medial lemniscus lie medially, in the medial medullary territory, so limb strength and proprioception are usually preserved. Both are shown without glow.

risks.why: Parent vessel; PICA usually arises from it (PICA not modelled).

indications: Vertebral artery atherothrombosis or dissection (dissection is an important cause in younger patients)
PICA occlusion
Less often: demyelination, haemorrhage or tumour
pearls: A crossed pattern (face on one side, body on the other) localises to the lateral medulla or caudal pons.
Assess swallowing before any oral intake: aspiration is a major early risk.
Neurosurgical red flag: an associated PICA-territory cerebellar infarct can swell, compress the fourth ventricle and cause hydrocephalus and brainstem compression.
pitfalls: Small brainstem infarcts can be missed on early diffusion-weighted MRI; repeat imaging if clinical suspicion persists.
Marked hemiparesis is not part of the pure syndrome and suggests medial extension or a second lesion.
