approaches.title: Medial medullary syndrome (Dejerine)
approaches.summary: Infarction of the left paramedian medulla, usually from occlusion of vertebral or anterior spinal artery branches. Gives a contralateral hemiparesis that spares the face, with an ipsilateral tongue palsy.
context: ^(middle cerebellar peduncle|superior cerebellar peduncle|inferior cerebellar peduncle [lr])$

steps.t: Paramedian medulla: the pyramid, medial lemniscus and hypoglossal fascicles lie side by side close to the midline. Supply comes from penetrating branches of the vertebral and anterior spinal arteries.

Corticospinal fibres in the pyramid (above the decussation): contralateral (right) arm and leg weakness. The face is spared because the fibres to the facial nucleus have already left the pathway in the pons.
Contralateral loss of vibration and joint-position sense. In the medulla the lemniscus is already crossed, so the left lemniscus serves the right body.
Ipsilateral tongue weakness: on protrusion the tongue deviates toward the side of the lesion. The hypoglossal nucleus and nerve are not modelled.

risks.label: Pyramid (corticospinal tract)
risks.why: Contralateral hemiparesis sparing the face.

risks.label: Medial lemniscus
risks.why: Contralateral loss of vibration and proprioception.

risks.label: Hypoglossal fascicles / nucleus
risks.why: Ipsilateral tongue weakness, deviation toward the lesion. Not modelled.

indications: Atherosclerosis of the vertebral artery or its paramedian branches
Vertebral artery dissection
Rarely bilateral, giving quadriparesis; a "heart-shaped" diffusion signal has been described
pearls: Tongue deviates toward the weak side (the side of the lesion); limbs are weak on the opposite side.
Unlike the lateral medullary syndrome, pain and temperature are usually spared.
pitfalls: Presentations are often partial; isolated pure motor hemiparesis from a medullary infarct can mimic a capsular lacune.
approaches.schematic: Lesion sphere is schematic; hypoglossal nucleus and nerve are not modelled. Tracts glow along their whole course.

refs.title: Medial Medullary Syndrome — StatPearls (Siddik, Singh, Gupta)

approaches.title: Ventral caudal pons (Millard–Gubler syndrome)
approaches.summary: A lesion of the left ventral caudal pons that catches the fascicles of the abducens and facial nerves as they run ventrally, and the corticospinal fibres in the basis pontis.
context: ^(middle cerebellar peduncle|superior cerebellar peduncle|inferior cerebellar peduncle [lr])$

steps.t: Ventral caudal pons, supplied by paramedian and short circumferential branches of the basilar artery.
Contralateral (right) hemiparesis.
Ipsilateral lower motor neurone facial palsy, involving forehead and lower face.
Ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy: horizontal diplopia worse looking to the left, failure of abduction. The abducens nerve is not modelled; its target muscle is shown (no glow).

risks.label: Corticospinal fibres
risks.why: Contralateral hemiparesis.

risks.label: Facial nerve fascicles
risks.why: Ipsilateral LMN facial palsy.

risks.label: Abducens nerve fascicles
risks.why: Ipsilateral abduction failure. Not modelled.

indications: Pontine infarction (basilar branch disease)
Haemorrhage, including cavernous malformation
Tumour (e.g. pontine glioma) and demyelination
pearls: A fascicular abducens palsy with a facial palsy and contralateral hemiparesis localises to the ventral caudal pons.
Eponym definitions vary: some sources call abducens palsy with contralateral hemiparesis alone "Raymond syndrome".
pitfalls: A gaze palsy (both eyes cannot look to one side) points instead to the abducens nucleus or PPRF in the dorsal pons, not the fascicle.
approaches.schematic: Lesion sphere is schematic; abducens nerve not modelled. Tracts and nerves glow along their whole course.

refs.title: Millard-Gubler Syndrome — StatPearls (Sakuru, Elnahry, Lui, Bollu)

approaches.title: Dorsal caudal pons: facial colliculus lesion (Foville)
approaches.summary: A lesion of the left floor of the fourth ventricle at the facial colliculus, where the facial nerve fibres loop around the abducens nucleus. Relevant to any surgery on the fourth-ventricle floor.
context: ^(middle cerebellar peduncle|superior cerebellar peduncle|inferior cerebellar peduncle [lr])$

steps.t: Facial colliculus on the floor of the fourth ventricle (lower pons). The fourth ventricle is shown faintly; the sphere marks the colliculus.
The internal genu of the facial nerve: ipsilateral lower motor neurone facial palsy.

Damage to the abducens nucleus (or the nearby PPRF) causes an ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy: neither eye can look to the left. The yoked muscles that fail together are shown: left lateral rectus and right medial rectus (no glow; the nucleus is not modelled).

If the medial longitudinal fasciculus is also involved, the result is a one-and-a-half syndrome. Ventral extension adds contralateral hemiparesis; that combination is often called Foville syndrome, although definitions vary between sources.

risks.label: Facial nerve genu
risks.why: Ipsilateral LMN facial palsy.

risks.label: Abducens nucleus / PPRF
risks.why: Ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy. Not modelled.

risks.label: Medial longitudinal fasciculus
risks.why: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia; with the above, one-and-a-half syndrome. Not modelled.

risks.label: Corticospinal fibres (if ventral extension)
risks.why: Contralateral hemiparesis.

indications: Pontine tegmental haemorrhage, including cavernous malformation
Infarction, demyelination, tumour
Surgical injury to the fourth-ventricle floor
pearls: Gaze palsy (nucleus) versus abduction palsy (nerve) is the key localising distinction.
In fourth-ventricle and brainstem surgery the facial colliculus is a landmark to avoid; entry zones above and below it are described in the literature. See the Telovelar approach card.
pitfalls: Facial colliculus syndrome is a clinical description of a region, not a single disease; image to find the cause.
approaches.schematic: Lesion sphere is schematic; abducens nucleus, PPRF and MLF are not modelled.

refs.title: Neuroanatomy, Facial Colliculus — StatPearls (Nem, Yoo, Omole)

approaches.title: Locked-in syndrome (bilateral ventral pons)
approaches.summary: Bilateral destruction of the ventral pons, classically from basilar artery occlusion. The patient is awake and aware but cannot move the limbs or face, or speak. Vertical eye movements and blinking are spared.
context: ^(middle cerebellar peduncle|superior cerebellar peduncle|inferior cerebellar peduncle [lr])$

steps.t: The basis pontis, supplied by the basilar artery (glowing). Occlusion of its paramedian branches destroys the ventral pons on both sides.
Both corticospinal tracts (quadriplegia) and both corticobulbar tracts (anarthria, dysphagia, facial weakness).

The tegmentum, including the reticular activating system, is spared, so consciousness is preserved. The midbrain is spared, so vertical gaze and lid elevation (oculomotor nerves) remain. Horizontal gaze is often lost. Sensation may be preserved.

risks.label: Corticospinal tracts, both sides
risks.why: Quadriplegia.

risks.label: Corticobulbar tracts, both sides
risks.why: Anarthria, dysphagia, facial paralysis.

risks.label: Abducens nuclei / PPRF (variable)
risks.why: Loss of horizontal gaze. Not modelled.

risks.label: Basilar artery
risks.why: Usual culprit vessel.

indications: Basilar artery thrombosis or embolism (most common)
Pontine haemorrhage
Osmotic demyelination (central pontine myelinolysis)
Trauma
pearls: Always test for awareness with vertical eye movement and blinking commands: an unresponsive patient may be fully aware.
Basilar occlusion is time-critical for reperfusion; prodromal symptoms are common.
pitfalls: Can be mistaken for coma or a vegetative state.
approaches.schematic: Lesion sphere is schematic. Tracts glow along their whole course; the lesion involves only their pontine segment.

approaches.title: Ventral midbrain (Weber syndrome)
approaches.summary: A lesion of the left cerebral peduncle catching the oculomotor fascicles. Gives an ipsilateral third nerve palsy with a contralateral hemiparesis.
context: ^(middle cerebellar peduncle|superior cerebellar peduncle|inferior cerebellar peduncle [lr])$

steps.t: Ventromedial midbrain (cerebral peduncle), supplied by paramedian perforators from the top of the basilar artery and the P1 segment of the posterior cerebral artery.
Ipsilateral third nerve palsy: ptosis, a dilated pupil, and the eye resting "down and out". The muscles that fail are shown. Superior oblique (CN IV) and lateral rectus (CN VI) are spared.
Corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres: contralateral (right) hemiparesis, including upper motor neurone weakness of the lower face and tongue.

risks.label: Oculomotor fascicles
risks.why: Ipsilateral ptosis, mydriasis, ophthalmoplegia.

risks.label: Corticospinal fibres
risks.why: Contralateral hemiparesis.

risks.label: Corticobulbar fibres
risks.why: Contralateral UMN facial and tongue weakness.

indications: Infarction of PCA or basilar perforators
Haemorrhage or tumour
Neurosurgical mimic: uncal herniation compressing the ipsilateral nerve and peduncle (see the uncal herniation card)
pearls: Third nerve palsy plus contralateral hemiparesis localises to the ipsilateral midbrain until proven otherwise.
pitfalls: A pupil-involving third nerve palsy without other signs suggests compression (e.g. a posterior communicating artery aneurysm), not a midbrain stroke: image the vessels.
approaches.schematic: Lesion sphere is schematic. Tracts and nerves glow along their whole course.

approaches.title: Paramedian midbrain tegmentum (Benedikt syndrome)
approaches.summary: A lesion of the left midbrain tegmentum involving the oculomotor fascicles and the red nucleus region. Gives an ipsilateral third nerve palsy with contralateral involuntary movements and ataxia.
context: ^(middle cerebellar peduncle|superior cerebellar peduncle|inferior cerebellar peduncle [lr])$

steps.t: Paramedian midbrain tegmentum at the level of the red nucleus, supplied by paramedian perforators of the basilar and P1 segments.
Ipsilateral third nerve palsy.

Red nucleus and crossed dentatorubrothalamic fibres: contralateral tremor, ataxia and involuntary movements (choreoathetosis). The fibres have already crossed in the caudal midbrain, so the signs are on the right.
Extension to the medial lemniscus adds contralateral sensory loss; extension to the cerebral peduncle adds contralateral hemiparesis.

risks.label: Oculomotor fascicles
risks.why: Ipsilateral third nerve palsy.

risks.label: Red nucleus region
risks.why: Contralateral tremor, ataxia, choreoathetosis.

risks.label: Medial lemniscus (variable)
risks.why: Contralateral loss of vibration and proprioception.

indications: Infarction (basilar or PCA perforators)
Haemorrhage, tumour, demyelination
pearls: Claude, Benedikt and Weber syndromes overlap: dorsal tegmentum gives ataxia (Claude), red nucleus gives added involuntary movements (Benedikt), and the ventral peduncle gives hemiparesis (Weber).
pitfalls: Clinical eponym boundaries are loose; describe the deficits and the imaging level rather than relying on the eponym.
approaches.schematic: Lesion sphere is schematic. Tracts and nerves glow along their whole course.

approaches.title: Dorsal midbrain tegmentum (Claude syndrome)
approaches.summary: A lesion of the left dorsal midbrain tegmentum involving the oculomotor fascicles and the cerebellar outflow (superior cerebellar peduncle fibres and dorsal red nucleus). Gives an ipsilateral third nerve palsy with contralateral ataxia.
context: ^(middle cerebellar peduncle|superior cerebellar peduncle|inferior cerebellar peduncle [lr])$

steps.t: Ipsilateral third nerve palsy.
Fibres of the superior cerebellar peduncle (glowing) and the dorsal red nucleus: contralateral limb ataxia and dysmetria.

risks.label: Oculomotor fascicles
risks.why: Ipsilateral third nerve palsy.

risks.label: Superior cerebellar peduncle fibres
risks.why: Contralateral ataxia.

risks.label: Red nucleus (dorsal part)
risks.why: Contralateral ataxia; tremor if more extensive (Benedikt overlap).

indications: Lacunar infarction of midbrain perforators
Less often haemorrhage, tumour or demyelination
pearls: Compare with the Benedikt and Weber cards: the deficits track the dorsal-to-ventral position of the lesion.
pitfalls: The superior cerebellar peduncle is modelled as a single midline structure here, so its glow is not side-specific.
approaches.schematic: Lesion sphere is schematic. Tracts and nerves glow along their whole course.

refs.title: Claude Syndrome: A Rare but Easily Recognizable Midbrain Lacunar Syndrome — Cureus 2025 (Carranza et al.)

approaches.title: Dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome
approaches.summary: Compression or damage of the dorsal midbrain (pretectum and posterior commissure). Gives a vertical gaze palsy, mainly of upgaze. A classic presentation of pineal region tumours and obstructive hydrocephalus.
context: ^(middle cerebellar peduncle|superior cerebellar peduncle|inferior cerebellar peduncle [lr])$

steps.t: Pineal region masses compress the tectal plate from behind and above. The pineal body is shown glowing as the "mass".

Vertical (especially upward) gaze palsy; convergence–retraction nystagmus on attempted upgaze; light–near dissociation of the pupils; eyelid retraction (Collier sign). The responsible pretectal nuclei and posterior commissure are not modelled; the superior colliculi mark the tectal plate.
Compression of the cerebral aqueduct causes obstructive hydrocephalus. Raised pressure itself can produce the same dorsal midbrain signs.

risks.label: Posterior commissure / pretectal nuclei
risks.why: Upgaze palsy, light–near dissociation, convergence–retraction nystagmus. Not modelled.

risks.label: Tectal plate (superior colliculi)
risks.why: Landmark of the compressed dorsal midbrain.

risks.label: Pineal body
risks.why: Site of pineal region tumours.

risks.label: Cerebral aqueduct
risks.why: Obstruction leads to hydrocephalus.

indications: Pineal region tumours (germ cell tumours, pineal parenchymal tumours, others)
Obstructive hydrocephalus, including shunt malfunction
Tectal glioma; midbrain haemorrhage or infarction; trauma
pearls: In a child with a shunt, new upgaze failure ("setting sun" eyes) should prompt assessment for shunt malfunction.
For pineal region masses, serum and CSF tumour markers (AFP, β-hCG) help identify germ cell tumours before surgery.
See the Supracerebellar infratentorial approach card and the pineal region Rhoton plates.
pitfalls: The superior colliculi are not themselves the cause of the gaze palsy; the critical structures are the pretectum and posterior commissure just rostral to them.
approaches.schematic: Lesion sphere is schematic; pretectal nuclei and posterior commissure are not modelled.

approaches.title: Cerebellopontine angle syndrome
approaches.summary: An extra-axial mass in the left cerebellopontine angle, most often a vestibular schwannoma. Deficits accumulate as the mass grows: the vestibulocochlear nerve first, then the trigeminal nerve, cerebellar peduncle and brainstem.
context: ^(middle cerebellar peduncle|superior cerebellar peduncle|inferior cerebellar peduncle [lr])$

steps.t: Unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance. These are the earliest and commonest symptoms.
The facial nerve is stretched and displaced, but clinical facial weakness before surgery is uncommon with schwannomas. Its preservation is the central surgical challenge.
Larger tumours reach the trigeminal nerve: facial numbness and a reduced corneal reflex.
Middle cerebellar peduncle and cerebellar compression: ipsilateral ataxia. Brainstem distortion and fourth-ventricle compression can cause obstructive hydrocephalus.

risks.label: Vestibulocochlear nerve
risks.why: Hearing loss, tinnitus, imbalance.

risks.label: Facial nerve
risks.why: Usually preserved before surgery; at risk during resection.

risks.label: Trigeminal nerve
risks.why: Facial numbness, reduced corneal reflex.

risks.label: Middle cerebellar peduncle
risks.why: Ipsilateral ataxia.

risks.label: Lower cranial nerves (large tumours)
risks.why: Dysphagia and hoarseness. Not modelled.

indications: Vestibular schwannoma (the most common CPA mass)
Meningioma, epidermoid cyst
Other schwannomas, metastases and rarer lesions
pearls: Unilateral sensorineural hearing loss warrants MRI of the internal acoustic meati.
See the Vestibular schwannoma case specimen, the Retrosigmoid and Translabyrinthine approach cards, and the posterior fossa Rhoton plates.
pitfalls: Early facial weakness or rapid progression is atypical for a schwannoma; consider meningioma, facial nerve schwannoma or malignancy.
approaches.schematic: The mass sphere is schematic; cranial nerves are population tractography reconstructions.

approaches.title: Thalamic sensory syndrome (Dejerine–Roussy)
approaches.summary: A lesion of the left ventral posterior thalamus. Gives contralateral loss of sensation, and weeks to months later contralateral central (thalamic) pain may develop.
context: ^(left|right) (pulvinar|internal medullary lamina|medial geniculate body|lateral geniculate body)$

steps.t: Inferolateral thalamus, supplied by thalamogeniculate branches of the posterior cerebral artery (not modelled).
VPL (body) and VPM (face): contralateral loss of sensation, all modalities, face and body.
Contralateral burning pain and allodynia can appear later and is often refractory. Mild hemiparesis (internal capsule), ataxia or involuntary movements may accompany it.

risks.label: VPL nucleus
risks.why: Contralateral body sensory loss; later central pain.

risks.label: VPM nucleus
risks.why: Contralateral facial sensory loss.

risks.label: Posterior limb of internal capsule (variable)
risks.why: Contralateral hemiparesis. Not modelled as a separate structure.

indications: Thalamic infarction (PCA thalamogeniculate branches)
Hypertensive thalamic haemorrhage
Tumour or other focal lesions
pearls: The pain often begins after partial sensory recovery.
Neuromodulation (e.g. motor cortex stimulation or deep brain stimulation) has been tried for refractory central pain, with variable results.
pitfalls: Not every post-stroke pain is thalamic; central post-stroke pain also follows brainstem and cortical lesions.
approaches.schematic: Lesion sphere is schematic; thalamic nuclei are from the SPL-PNL atlas.

refs.title: Thalamic Pain Syndrome — StatPearls (Stretanski, Hu, Munakomi)

approaches.title: Artery of Percheron infarction
approaches.summary: A single arterial trunk arising from one P1 segment supplies both paramedian thalami, and sometimes the rostral midbrain. Its occlusion causes bilateral paramedian thalamic infarction.
context: ^(left|right) (pulvinar|internal medullary lamina|medial geniculate body|lateral geniculate body)$

steps.t: Dorsomedial and intralaminar nuclei on both sides: reduced consciousness or hypersomnolence, memory impairment, and behavioural change (abulia, apathy).
Midbrain involvement adds vertical gaze palsy and oculomotor signs. A V-shaped midbrain signal on FLAIR/diffusion imaging has been described.

risks.label: Dorsomedial nuclei
risks.why: Memory and behavioural change.

risks.label: Intralaminar nuclei / internal medullary lamina
risks.why: Reduced arousal.

risks.label: Rostral midbrain (variable)
risks.why: Vertical gaze palsy, oculomotor signs.

indications: Embolic or small-vessel occlusion of the artery of Percheron variant
pearls: Consider this in unexplained reduced consciousness with a normal CT: diffusion MRI is diagnostic.
Differentials of bilateral thalamic change include deep cerebral venous thrombosis (internal cerebral veins), top-of-basilar occlusion and some metabolic or infective encephalopathies.
pitfalls: Early CT is often normal.
approaches.schematic: Lesion spheres are schematic.

refs.title: Clinical review and analysis of artery of Percheron infarction — IBRO Neurosci Rep 2023 (Li, Ge, Yang, Yao)

approaches.title: Foster Kennedy syndrome
approaches.summary: A left frontal base mass compresses the left optic nerve, causing optic atrophy on that side. Raised intracranial pressure causes papilloedema in the other eye. Anosmia on the side of the mass is common.
context: ^(left|right) (lateral|medial|superior|inferior) rectus$|^(left|right) superior oblique$|^(left|right) levator palpebrae superioris$

steps.t: Anterior cranial base, under the left frontal lobe (gyrus rectus shown). Classic causes are olfactory groove and medial sphenoid wing meningiomas.
Direct compression of the left optic nerve: visual loss and optic atrophy in the left eye.
Raised intracranial pressure: disc swelling in the right eye. The atrophic left disc cannot swell.
Olfactory bulb and tract compression on the side of the mass: unilateral anosmia, often unnoticed by the patient. The olfactory tract is not modelled.

risks.label: Left optic nerve
risks.why: Ipsilateral visual loss and optic atrophy.

risks.label: Olfactory bulb and tract
risks.why: Ipsilateral anosmia. Not modelled.

risks.label: Raised intracranial pressure
risks.why: Contralateral papilloedema.

indications: Olfactory groove meningioma
Medial sphenoid wing meningioma
Other frontal base tumours
pearls: Test smell in any patient with unexplained unilateral optic atrophy.
A "pseudo-Foster Kennedy" picture, for example sequential ischaemic optic neuropathy, is often more frequent than the true syndrome.
See the Bifrontal and Supraorbital approach cards and the anterior fossa Rhoton plates.
pitfalls: Bilateral disc swelling with one atrophic disc can be misread as asymmetric papilloedema.
approaches.schematic: The mass sphere is schematic.

approaches.title: Cavernous sinus syndrome
approaches.summary: Disease of the left cavernous sinus affects the nerves that pass through it: CN III, IV, V1 (sometimes V2), and VI. It also affects the sympathetic fibres on the internal carotid artery. Gives a painful or painless ophthalmoplegia with upper facial numbness.
context: ^(left|right) (lateral|medial|superior|inferior) rectus$|^(left|right) superior oblique$|^(left|right) levator palpebrae superioris$

steps.t: Lateral to the sella and pituitary, around the cavernous internal carotid artery. The sphere marks the left sinus.
CN III (glowing), IV and VI (not modelled): ophthalmoplegia, diplopia and ptosis. All the extraocular muscles of the left eye are shown, because any of them can fail.
steps.show: ^left (lateral|medial|superior|inferior) rectus$|^left superior oblique$|^left levator palpebrae superioris$

steps.t: V1, and sometimes V2: numbness of the forehead (and cheek) and a reduced corneal reflex. The whole trigeminal nerve glows; only its first two divisions run in or along the sinus.

Horner syndrome; with a third nerve palsy as well, the pupil may be mid-sized. Venous obstruction or a carotid–cavernous fistula adds proptosis, chemosis and an orbital bruit. Vision is usually spared, unlike the orbital apex syndrome.

risks.label: Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
risks.why: Ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, pupil involvement.

risks.label: Trochlear nerve (CN IV)
risks.why: Superior oblique weakness. Not modelled.

risks.label: Abducens nerve (CN VI)
risks.why: Abduction failure; often the first nerve affected because it lies freely within the sinus. Not modelled.

risks.label: Trigeminal V1 (± V2)
risks.why: Forehead and cheek numbness, reduced corneal reflex.

risks.label: Cavernous internal carotid artery
risks.why: Aneurysm or fistula source; carries the sympathetic plexus.

indications: Pituitary adenoma with lateral extension; pituitary apoplexy
Meningioma, metastasis, lymphoma
Carotid–cavernous fistula; cavernous carotid aneurysm
Cavernous sinus thrombosis (often septic)
Inflammation, e.g. Tolosa–Hunt syndrome (a diagnosis of exclusion)
pearls: The abducens nerve is often affected early because it lies within the sinus next to the carotid, rather than in the lateral wall.
See the Pterional, Orbitozygomatic, Kawase and endonasal approach cards and the cavernous sinus Rhoton plates.
pitfalls: Visual loss means the lesion extends to the orbital apex or optic canal.
approaches.schematic: Lesion sphere is schematic; CN IV, CN VI and the sympathetic plexus are not modelled.

approaches.title: Superior orbital fissure and orbital apex syndromes
approaches.summary: A lesion at the left superior orbital fissure affects CN III, IV, VI and V1. When the lesion extends to the orbital apex, the optic nerve is affected too and vision is threatened.
context: ^(left|right) (lateral|medial|superior|inferior) rectus$|^(left|right) superior oblique$|^(left|right) levator palpebrae superioris$

steps.t: CN III (glowing), IV and VI: ophthalmoplegia and ptosis. V1: forehead numbness. Superior ophthalmic vein: proptosis. Vision is spared.
steps.show: ^left (lateral|medial|superior|inferior) rectus$|^left superior oblique$|^left levator palpebrae superioris$

steps.t: Adds the optic nerve in the optic canal: reduced acuity, a relative afferent pupillary defect and visual field loss.

risks.label: Oculomotor nerve (CN III)
risks.why: Ptosis, ophthalmoplegia.

risks.label: Trochlear and abducens nerves
risks.why: Ophthalmoplegia. Not modelled.

risks.label: Ophthalmic nerve (V1)
risks.why: Forehead numbness, reduced corneal reflex. Only the trigeminal root is modelled.

risks.label: Optic nerve (apex only)
risks.why: Visual loss, RAPD.

indications: Trauma (orbital and skull base fractures)
Inflammation, e.g. IgG4-related disease or sarcoidosis
Infection: invasive fungal sinusitis is an emergency, especially in diabetic or immunocompromised patients
Neoplasm (local or metastatic); vascular lesions
pearls: Vision separates the orbital apex syndrome from the superior orbital fissure and cavernous sinus syndromes: check acuity and pupils.
See the Orbitozygomatic approach card and the orbit and orbital apex Rhoton plates.
pitfalls: A painful ophthalmoplegia in a diabetic patient with sinus disease must be treated as invasive fungal infection until proven otherwise.
approaches.schematic: Lesion spheres are schematic; CN IV, CN VI and V1 branches are not modelled.

approaches.title: Gradenigo syndrome (petrous apicitis)
approaches.summary: Infection of the left petrous apex, usually complicating otitis media or mastoiditis. The classic triad is otorrhoea, deep facial or retro-orbital pain, and an ipsilateral abducens palsy. The full triad is often incomplete.
context: ^(left|right) (lateral|medial|superior|inferior) rectus$|^(left|right) superior oblique$|^(left|right) levator palpebrae superioris$

steps.t: The sphere marks the left petrous apex, near Dorello’s canal (CN VI) and Meckel’s cave (trigeminal ganglion).
Irritation gives deep facial and retro-orbital pain in the trigeminal (mainly V1) distribution.
The abducens nerve is compressed or inflamed in Dorello’s canal: ipsilateral lateral rectus palsy (the nerve is not modelled; its muscle is shown).

risks.label: Trigeminal ganglion (Meckel’s cave)
risks.why: Retro-orbital and facial pain.

risks.label: Abducens nerve in Dorello’s canal
risks.why: Ipsilateral abduction failure. Not modelled.

risks.label: Middle ear and mastoid
risks.why: Otorrhoea, otalgia. Not modelled.

indications: Petrous apicitis complicating acute or chronic otitis media or mastoiditis
Differentials of petrous apex lesions: cholesterol granuloma, cholesteatoma, tumours
pearls: Image with CT of the temporal bones and contrast MRI; look for venous sinus thrombosis, meningitis and abscess.
See the Kawase and middle fossa Rhoton plates for petrous apex anatomy.
pitfalls: A sixth nerve palsy is a false localising sign of raised pressure; with ear disease, think of the petrous apex.
approaches.schematic: Lesion sphere is schematic; abducens nerve and middle ear are not modelled.

refs.title: The Diagnosis, Management, and Outcomes of Gradenigo Syndrome in Children: A Scoping Review — Diagnostics (Basel) 2025 (Schmit et al.)

approaches.title: Jugular foramen syndromes (Vernet, Collet–Sicard)
approaches.summary: Lesions of the left jugular foramen affect CN IX, X and XI (Vernet syndrome). Extension to the hypoglossal canal adds CN XII (Collet–Sicard syndrome).
context: ^(left|right) (lateral|medial|superior|inferior) rectus$|^(left|right) superior oblique$|^(left|right) levator palpebrae superioris$

steps.t: Between the petrous temporal and occipital bones, where the sigmoid sinus becomes the internal jugular vein. The nerves are not modelled; the sphere marks the foramen.
Dysphagia, hoarseness from ipsilateral vocal-cord palsy, a reduced gag reflex, palatal droop with the uvula pulled away from the lesion, and loss of taste on the posterior third of the tongue.
Weakness and wasting of the ipsilateral sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles (shown).
Extension to the hypoglossal canal: ipsilateral tongue weakness. Additional sympathetic involvement (Horner syndrome) points to the retrostyloid space (Villaret syndrome).

risks.label: Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX)
risks.why: Dysphagia, reduced gag, posterior tongue taste loss. Not modelled.

risks.label: Vagus nerve (X)
risks.why: Hoarseness, vocal-cord palsy, palatal weakness. Not modelled.

risks.label: Accessory nerve (XI)
risks.why: Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius weakness (muscle shown; nerve not modelled).

risks.label: Hypoglossal nerve (XII)
risks.why: Tongue weakness (Collet–Sicard). Not modelled.

risks.label: Internal jugular vein / sigmoid sinus
risks.why: Venous structure through the foramen; thrombosis or tumour invasion.

indications: Paraganglioma (glomus jugulare)
Schwannomas of IX–XI, meningioma, metastasis
Skull base fracture
Internal carotid artery dissection and jugular vein thrombosis have been reported
pearls: See the Far-lateral approach card and the jugular foramen Rhoton plates.
pitfalls: Bilateral or progressive lower cranial nerve palsies with normal brainstem imaging need dedicated skull base and neck imaging.
approaches.schematic: Lesion spheres are schematic; cranial nerves IX–XII are not modelled.

approaches.title: Gerstmann syndrome (dominant inferior parietal lobule)
approaches.summary: A lesion of the dominant (usually left) inferior parietal lobule, classically the angular gyrus. Gives the tetrad of agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia and left–right disorientation.
context: ^(left|right) (supramarginal gyrus|superior parietal lobule|postcentral gyrus|superior temporal gyrus|lateral occipital gyrus)$

steps.t: Agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia and left–right disorientation. The pure tetrad is rare; it is usually accompanied by aphasia, alexia or apraxia.
Disconnection of parietal association fibres has been proposed as a mechanism in some cases. The superior longitudinal fasciculus III and arcuate fasciculus are shown for orientation.

risks.label: Left inferior parietal lobule (angular gyrus)

approaches.title: Uncal herniation and the Kernohan notch phenomenon
approaches.summary: A left supratentorial mass pushes the medial temporal lobe (uncus) through the tentorial incisura. The usual picture is an ipsilateral third nerve palsy with contralateral hemiparesis. In the Kernohan notch phenomenon, the opposite cerebral peduncle is pressed against the tentorial edge, so the hemiparesis is on the same side as the mass.
context: ^(middle cerebellar peduncle|superior cerebellar peduncle|inferior cerebellar peduncle [lr])$

steps.t: The uncus (ambiens and parahippocampal gyri shown) herniates medially over the tentorial edge.
The left oculomotor nerve is compressed: the pupil dilates first (its parasympathetic fibres are superficial), followed by ptosis and ophthalmoplegia.
Compression of the left cerebral peduncle: right-sided (contralateral) hemiparesis.
The midbrain is displaced so that the right peduncle is notched by the right tentorial edge: left-sided hemiparesis, on the same side as the mass. This is a false localising sign.
Posterior cerebral artery compression causes occipital infarction. Downward brainstem displacement can tear perforators (Duret haemorrhages). Aqueduct compression causes hydrocephalus.

risks.label: Ipsilateral oculomotor nerve
risks.why: Dilated pupil, then ptosis and ophthalmoplegia.

risks.label: Ipsilateral cerebral peduncle
risks.why: Contralateral hemiparesis (usual).

risks.label: Contralateral cerebral peduncle
risks.why: Ipsilateral hemiparesis (Kernohan notch, false localising).

risks.label: Posterior cerebral artery
risks.why: Occipital infarction. Not separately modelled.

indications: Acute subdural or extradural haematoma
Temporal lobe haemorrhage, contusion or tumour
Any rapidly expanding supratentorial mass
pearls: The dilated pupil is usually the more reliable lateralising sign; a hemiparesis can be falsely localising.
This is time-critical: treat raised pressure and evacuate the mass as indicated.
pitfalls: In trauma, decide the side of surgery on imaging, not on the side of the hemiparesis alone.
A dilated pupil can also come from direct orbital or ocular trauma, or from drugs.
